title: Poured fondant glaze
subtitle: smooth opaque fondant coating for petits fours and iced cakes
excerpt: Poured fondant glaze is a smooth, opaque, white sugar coating made from fondant loosened with a little sugar syrup and warmed until pourable. It sets to a matte finish with a very slight sheen and a thin, firm shell. This is the classic coating for English iced fancies, petits fours glacés, and fondant-iced small cakes, not to be confused with rolled fondant, which is worked by hand, or mirror glaze, which is gelatine-based.
sourceNotes: Poured fondant has been used in British and French confectionery and pâtisserie for at least two centuries. In Britain, it appears in Victorian baking books as the coating for 'fondant fancies', small square sponge cakes coated in coloured fondant. The same technique is used in French pâtisserie for petit fours glacés, where small marzipan or cake pieces are dipped or poured with fondant. The essential technique, warming block fondant or making fondant from syrup, diluting to coating consistency, and pouring or dipping, is unchanged from 19th-century recipes, though modern block fondant (available commercially) eliminates the need to cook fondant from scratch.

recipe.makeAheadNotes: The glaze can be rewarmed if it sets in the bowl; add a teaspoon more syrup if needed to loosen.
recipe.temperatureNote: working temperature for the fondant glaze; above 43°C the fondant turns dull on setting

content.text: Poured fondant glaze gives petits fours and small iced cakes a smooth, opaque, slightly shiny coating that sets firm. The critical control is temperature: too hot and the fondant sets dull; too cool and it won't flow across the surface. Work at 38,40°C, measured with a thermometer. If it sets in the bowl before you're done, set the bowl back over warm water for 30 seconds and stir to loosen.

items.prepNote: optional; gel or paste colours only

content.text: Bring the water and sugar to the boil in a small saucepan, stir to dissolve, and remove from the heat. This light syrup dilutes the fondant to pouring consistency. You may not use all of it, add gradually and stop when the texture is right.

Break the block fondant into pieces and place in a heatproof bowl set over a pan of barely simmering water. Stir gently as it melts. Do not allow the fondant to exceed 43°C, above this temperature the sugar crystals re-melt, and the coating will set dull rather than with the characteristic slight sheen. Check with a probe thermometer. Add syrup a tablespoon at a time, stirring between each addition, until the fondant is the consistency of double cream, it flows from the spoon in a ribbon and doesn't hold peaks. Add any food colouring now, stirring thoroughly.
Coat the cakes or petits fours

Set the items to be coated on a wire rack over a tray to catch drips. Work quickly, the fondant sets within a few minutes of leaving the bowl. Pour or spoon the glaze over each piece from the centre outward, letting gravity pull it to the edges and sides. For small items, dip them briefly upside down into the glaze and allow the excess to drip off. Leave to set at room temperature for at least 1 hour before handling. Once set, the surface will be matte-smooth with a slight sheen.
